title: Marriage, Jacksonville concert band and the Uncle Tom's Cabin job in New York
summary: After marrying the president's daughter White worked as a printer and led the Jacksonville Concert Band until Mr. Jenkins called him back to take a unit to New York.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: After my marriage to the president's daughter, Roxabel, I took residence in Jacksonville. And my first job was as a printer with the Florida Union Printing Company. Mrs. Saunders owned it. She was a very wealthy Negro woman down there. And this office had been the former office of one of the noted Negro writers, T. Thomas Fortune, whom the world recognizes as one of the greatest editorialists of his day and time. So I worked there for about 10 months. While in Jacksonville, the second biggest band in Jacksonville, numbering about, I suppose, 15 pieces, asked me to become their leader. And that band was the Jacksonville Concert Band. And under Castellana and Dean, realtors in Jacksonville, they established a park out on Davis Street in Jacksonville, Florida, building up a new section out there, residential, for the Negroes of Jacksonville, Florida. The Negro population had begun to grow extensively. Castellana and Dean, biggest realtors in town, cut out this whole plot out there. I suppose, very near, oh, possibly 80 acres or more. And they built a fine band standing around. And every Sunday afternoon, the Jacksonville Concert Band, we gave concerts in this pavilion. For a while, I thought Jacksonville was going to be a really fine place for me. But the old man, whom we called, the old man is Mr. Jenkins, my father-in-law, called me back to Charleston. Everything is reconciled now. So we're on good terms again. And he called me back to Charleston. And he says, take the band to New York, and Edmund will meet you there. This is the second year for Edmund's directorship of the band. Edmund is my brother-in-law, Edmund Jenkins. When Edmund came, he says, I'd rather you take a portion of the band. Now we had about 44 pieces this year, bigger than ever. I want you to take a portion of the band. I want you to take a portion of the band. I want you to take a small unit of it and play this Uncle Tom's Cabin production.
At the old Columbia Theater. I think it was on 47th Street, I don't remember where. Oh, right on Broadway. Yeah. Yeah, I remember.
